elabc.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). WHAT GREEK A1 ASKS OF A READER, counted on its {fact.a1Words} headwords: {fact.pairWords} hold a two-letter spelling and cannot be read one letter at a time; {fact.spelledWords} hold an [i], an [e] or an [o] written otherwise than ι, ε or ο, which no rule predicts; {fact.accentWords} carry the accent; {fact.sigmaWords} end in ς; {fact.capitalWords} are written with a capital, the days and the months; and {fact.questionSentences} of A1's example sentences end in the Greek question mark. THE PACE: Folio deals ten new cards a day to a language deck unless you change it in the deck's options. A letter, a pair or a sign is two cards and a reading rule is one, so these {notes} notes are {cards} cards, {days} days; Greek A1 then runs from day {greeka1.from} to day {greeka1.to}.

greeka1.subtitle: {notes} words and phrases · both directions, as two cards each
descSub: The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first.
The cards are dealt in a teaching order, described at the end of this text.
greeka1.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). {fact.added} cards were added to the {fact.generated} described above, each built from its own English Wiktionary entry by the same rules: the phrases of a first conversation (γεια σου and γεια σας, τι κάνεις and τι κάνετε, με λένε, πώς σε λένε, χαίρω πολύ, τα λέμε), what a traveller needs on the first day (δεν καταλαβαίνω, δεν ξέρω, πόσο κάνει, τι ώρα είναι), zero, thirteen to nineteen, forty and sixty to ninety. That makes {notes} notes, {cards} cards. THE ORDER: the first {fact.head} notes are set by hand — a greeting, thank you, please, yes and no on days 1 and 2, how are you on day {fact.howAreYouDay}, my name is on day {fact.nameDay}, the personal pronouns on days {fact.pronounsFrom} and {fact.pronounsTo}, to be and to have and the small words every sentence is built of, the commonest verbs on days {fact.verbsFrom} to {fact.verbsTo}, the question words on days {fact.questionsFrom} and {fact.questionsTo}, zero to ten on days {fact.zeroDay} to {fact.tenDay} — and the rest follow by frequency, with eleven to a thousand together from note {fact.numbersFrom}, the days of the week from note {fact.weekdaysFrom} with the months behind them, and the colours from note {fact.coloursFrom}. THE PACE: Folio deals ten new cards a day to a language deck unless you change it in the deck's options, both directions together, which is five words a day: this deck is {days} days, days {from} to {to} for a reader who takes the Greek Alphabet first. WHAT A CARD SHOWS: all {fact.nouns} nouns their article and gender, {fact.nounTables} of them the four cases in both numbers behind All forms, {fact.stressMoves} a genitive or plural marked "stress moves"; {fact.verbsAfterNa} of the {fact.verbs} verbs the six forms that follow θα and να; {fact.ipa} cards Wiktionary's pronunciation. On {fact.romanMisread} cards the romanisation holds a pair that is not said as English would say it (ai, ei, oi, y, nt, mp, gk): trust the pronunciation line and the speaker. WHERE THIS DECK ENDS, since it is the last Greek deck on the shelf: the example sentences are Tatoeba's, {fact.sentenceMedian} words long at the median. In the order the cards arrive, {fact.metPct}% of a sentence's words have been met by the time its card is dealt — a form counting as met only if a card shows it — and {fact.wholeSentences} of the {fact.sentences} sentences can be read whole. {fact.noCardPct}% of the words in these sentences are on no card of this deck: names such as Τομ, and words and forms beyond it. No A2 deck and no phrases deck has been built for Greek, so a reader who finishes here can greet, ask, count and read short sentences, and will meet unknown words in almost any text.
